level.title: Storage & Networking Fundamentals
level.description: Understand how data is stored and moved in the cloud — from object storage and block volumes to VPCs, subnets, and content delivery networks.

lessons.title: Cloud Storage: Object vs Block vs File
lessons.content_md:
# Cloud Storage: Object vs Block vs File

Cloud providers offer three fundamentally different storage paradigms. Choosing the right one is critical for performance, cost, and architecture.

## Object Storage

Stores data as discrete **objects** in a flat namespace (no folder hierarchy). Each object has a unique key, the data itself, and rich metadata.

**Best for:** Unstructured data — images, videos, backups, logs, data lake files.

| Provider | Service |
|----------|---------|
| AWS | S3 |
| GCP | Cloud Storage |
| Azure | Blob Storage |

```bash
# Upload a file to S3
aws s3 cp report.pdf s3://my-bucket/reports/2024/report.pdf

# List objects
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/reports/
```

**Key properties:**
- Virtually unlimited capacity
- 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability
- Access via HTTP/REST API
- Cannot be mounted as a filesystem (without adapters)
- Eventually consistent (some providers now offer strong consistency)

## Block Storage

Provides raw storage **volumes** that attach to compute instances, behaving like physical hard drives.

**Best for:** Databases, boot volumes, applications requiring low-latency I/O.

| Provider | Service |
|----------|---------|
| AWS | EBS (Elastic Block Store) |
| GCP | Persistent Disks |
| Azure | Managed Disks |

```bash
# Create a 100GB SSD volume (AWS)
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type gp3 \
  --size 100 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a
```

**Key properties:**
- Fixed size (must provision capacity)
- Attached to a single instance at a time
- Supports filesystem formatting (ext4, NTFS)
- Low latency, high throughput

## File Storage

Provides a shared **filesystem** accessible by multiple instances simultaneously via NFS or SMB protocols.

**Best for:** Shared application data, CMS content, legacy workloads requiring POSIX access.

| Provider | Service |
|----------|---------|
| AWS | EFS (Elastic File System) |
| GCP | Filestore |
| Azure | Azure Files |

## Quick Decision Matrix

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Store millions of images | Object Storage |
| Run a PostgreSQL database | Block Storage |
| Share config files across 10 servers | File Storage |
| Build a data lake | Object Storage |
| Boot an operating system | Block Storage |

lessons.title: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) & Subnets
lessons.content_md:
# Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) & Subnets

A VPC is your own **isolated, private network** inside the cloud. Think of it as building your own data center — but without the physical hardware.

## Why VPCs Matter

Without a VPC, all your cloud resources would sit on a shared, public network. A VPC gives you:
- **Isolation**: Your resources are invisible to other cloud tenants.
- **Control**: You define IP ranges, subnets, routing, and firewall rules.
- **Security**: Resources in private subnets have zero internet exposure by default.

## Core Concepts

### CIDR Blocks

VPCs use CIDR notation to define their IP address space:

```
10.0.0.0/16  →  65,536 IP addresses (10.0.0.0 – 10.0.255.255)
10.0.1.0/24  →  256 IP addresses   (10.0.1.0 – 10.0.1.255)
10.0.1.0/28  →  16 IP addresses    (10.0.1.0 – 10.0.1.15)
```

The smaller the number after `/`, the larger the network.

### Subnets

Subnets divide your VPC into smaller segments, typically organized by:
- **Public subnets**: Have a route to an Internet Gateway. Used for web servers, load balancers.
- **Private subnets**: No direct internet access. Used for databases, internal services.

```
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16
├── Public Subnet:  10.0.1.0/24  (web servers)
├── Public Subnet:  10.0.2.0/24  (load balancers)
├── Private Subnet: 10.0.10.0/24 (app servers)
└── Private Subnet: 10.0.20.0/24 (databases)
```

### Route Tables

Every subnet has a route table that determines where traffic goes:

```
Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local          ← traffic within the VPC
0.0.0.0/0       igw-abc123     ← internet (public subnet only)
```

### Security Groups vs NACLs

| Feature | Security Group | Network ACL |
|---------|---------------|-------------|
| Level | Instance (ENI) | Subnet |
| State | Stateful | Stateless |
| Rules | Allow only | Allow & Deny |
| Evaluation | All rules evaluated | Rules evaluated in order |

```bash
# AWS: Create a security group allowing HTTP traffic
aws ec2 create-security-group \
  --group-name web-sg \
  --description "Allow HTTP" \
  --vpc-id vpc-abc123

aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xyz789 \
  --protocol tcp \
  --port 80 \
  --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
```

## Best Practice: The 3-Tier Architecture

```
Internet → Load Balancer (public subnet)
             → App Servers (private subnet)
                → Database (private subnet, no internet)
```

This ensures your database is never directly reachable from the internet.

lessons.title: CDNs & Edge Computing
lessons.content_md:
# CDNs & Edge Computing

## The Latency Problem

If your server is in Virginia and your user is in Tokyo, every request travels ~11,000 km. At the speed of light through fiber, that's ~110ms round-trip — *just for physics*. Add DNS, TLS handshakes, and processing, and you're looking at 300-500ms per request.

**CDNs solve this by bringing content closer to the user.**

## Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)

A CDN is a globally distributed network of **edge servers** (Points of Presence, or PoPs) that cache and serve content from the location nearest to the user.

### How It Works

```
1. User in Tokyo requests image.jpg
2. CDN checks: is image.jpg cached at the Tokyo PoP?
   → YES: Serve immediately (~20ms)
   → NO:  Fetch from origin server, cache it, then serve (~300ms first time)
3. Next user in Tokyo gets it from cache (~20ms)
```

### Major CDN Services

| Provider | Service |
|----------|---------|
| AWS | CloudFront |
| GCP | Cloud CDN |
| Azure | Azure CDN |
| Independent | Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai |

### What CDNs Cache

- **Static assets**: Images, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, videos
- **API responses**: With appropriate cache headers
- **Entire pages**: For static sites

### Cache-Control Headers

```http
# Cache for 1 year (static assets with hashed filenames)
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Cache for 5 minutes (dynamic API data)
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, s-maxage=600

# Never cache (private user data)
Cache-Control: private, no-store
```

## Edge Computing

Edge computing goes beyond caching — it runs **code at the edge**, closer to the user.

### Use Cases

| Use Case | Example |
|----------|---------|
| URL rewriting | A/B test routing at the edge |
| Auth checks | Validate JWTs before hitting origin |
| Image optimization | Resize on-the-fly per device |
| Geolocation | Serve region-specific content |

### Edge Runtimes

| Provider | Service |
|----------|---------|
| AWS | Lambda@Edge / CloudFront Functions |
| Cloudflare | Workers |
| Vercel | Edge Functions |
| Deno | Deno Deploy |

```javascript
// Cloudflare Worker — redirect mobile users
export default {
  async fetch(request) {
    const userAgent = request.headers.get('User-Agent') || '';
    if (/Mobile/i.test(userAgent)) {
      return Response.redirect('https://m.example.com', 302);
    }
    return fetch(request);
  }
};
```

## CDN vs Edge Computing

| CDN | Edge Computing |
|-----|----------------|
| Caches static content | Runs dynamic logic |
| Read-only | Read + Write |
| Simple config | Requires code |
| Millisecond delivery | Millisecond computation |

lessons.title: Hands-On: Securing an S3 Bucket
lessons.content_md:
# Hands-On: Securing an S3 Bucket

S3 buckets are one of the most commonly misconfigured cloud resources. Unsecured buckets have led to massive data breaches at major companies. Let's learn how to lock one down properly.

## Step 1: Create a Bucket

```bash
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket my-secure-bucket-2024 \
  --region us-east-1
```

## Step 2: Block All Public Access

This is the **single most important** security setting:

```bash
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket my-secure-bucket-2024 \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
    BlockPublicAcls=true,\
    IgnorePublicAcls=true,\
    BlockPublicPolicy=true,\
    RestrictPublicBuckets=true
```

## Step 3: Enable Encryption

Encrypt all objects at rest using AES-256:

```bash
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
  --bucket my-secure-bucket-2024 \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{
    "Rules": [{
      "ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault": {
        "SSEAlgorithm": "AES256"
      },
      "BucketKeyEnabled": true
    }]
  }'
```

## Step 4: Enable Versioning

Versioning protects against accidental deletion and overwrites:

```bash
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket my-secure-bucket-2024 \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
```

## Step 5: Enable Access Logging

Track who accessed what and when:

```bash
aws s3api put-bucket-logging \
  --bucket my-secure-bucket-2024 \
  --bucket-logging-status '{
    "LoggingEnabled": {
      "TargetBucket": "my-log-bucket",
      "TargetPrefix": "s3-access-logs/"
    }
  }'
```

## Step 6: Apply a Restrictive Bucket Policy

Only allow access from your specific AWS account:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyUnencryptedUploads",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket-2024/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "AES256"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyHTTP",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket-2024",
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket-2024/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Security Checklist

- [x] Public access blocked
- [x] Server-side encryption enabled
- [x] Versioning enabled
- [x] Access logging enabled
- [x] Bucket policy enforces encryption & HTTPS
- [ ] Lifecycle rules for old versions (cost optimization)
- [ ] Cross-region replication (disaster recovery)

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---------|-------------|
| Public bucket policy | Anyone on the internet can download your data |
| No encryption | Data readable if storage media is compromised |
| No versioning | Accidental deletion is permanent |
| Overly broad IAM | Compromised credentials = full access |
